                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And Joseph nourished his father and his bre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thren, and all his fathers houshold with bread, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> as a little child is nou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rished.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> accord<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to the li<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>le ones.</ns0:note> according to <ns0:hi>their</ns0:hi> families <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>According to the mouth of the Family: mouth</ns0:hi> being put for their will or desire, as it is <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 24. 57. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 30. 2. as much as every one desired, without any restraint: Or, <ns0:hi>accord<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to the manner of a little child,</ns0:hi> he put their meat into their very mouths, it was brought to them without any more care or pains of theirs than an infant takes for its food.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And there was no bread in all the land: for the famine was very sore, so that the land of Egypt, and all the land of Canaan fainted by reason of the famine <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> Whence came it that the people in this extremity did not take the corn by force out of the several storehouses! <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> Besides that singular providence of God which watcheth over Kings and Rulers, and stilleth the tumults of the people, <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> had no doubt foreseen this difficulty and took due care to prevent it, partly by disposing the stores in strong and well guarded places; partly by adding wealth and strength to the King, whereby he might more easily suppress any seditious ri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sings; and principally by not permitting the people to despair or come to the utmost extremity, but giving them relief in all their exigencies.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And Joseph gathered up all the money, that was found in the land of Egypt <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Wherein he did no more than any of the Subjects might have done: he bought great store of Corn in the plentiful years with the Kings money<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and kept it till a time of Famine, and sold it at a rate which was agreeable to the season.</ns0:note>, and in the land of Canaan, for the corn which they bought: and Joseph brought the money into Pharaohs house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And when money failed in the land of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:44" />
unto Joseph, and said, Give us bread: for why should we die <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Why shouldest thou see and suffer us to perish for our want of money, when thou canst relieve us?</ns0:note> in thy presence? for the money faileth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And Joseph said, Give your cattle: and I will give for your cattle, if money fail.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And they brought their cattle unto Joseph: and Joseph gave them bread <ns0:hi>in exchange</ns0:hi> for horses, and for the flocks, and for the cattle of their herds, and for the asses, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> led them.</ns0:note> he fed them with bread, for all their cattle, for that year.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 When that year was ended, they came unto him the second year <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Not the second from the beginning of the Famine, but from their great extremity, the second year after that last men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioned, wherein they had sold their Cattle; but this seems to have been the last year of the Famine, because he now gives them Corn for food and for seed too, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 23. whereas in the six first years there was no sowing nor reaping, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 45. 6.</ns0:note>, and said unto him, We will not hide it from my lord, how that our money is spent, my lord also had our herds of cattle: there is not ought left in the sight of my lord, but our bodies, and our lands.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 Wherefore shall we die before thine eyes <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Whilst thou lookest upon us like an idle spectatour, not pitying and relieving us!</ns0:note>, both we and our land <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The land is said to die impro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perly, when it is desolate and barren, and when the fruits of it dye, or which is equivalent to it, do not live.</ns0:note>? buy us and our land for bread, and we and our land will be servants unto Pharaoh <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Pharaoh</ns0:hi> shall be the sole proprietor and we are content to be his Tenants to manage it for his use.</ns0:note>: and give <ns0:hi>us</ns0:hi> seed <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Because this was the last year of Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mine, as <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> informed them, and therefore they tilled and sowed the ground for the following year.</ns0:note> that we may live and not die, that the land be not desolate <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Without inhabitants, as it will be if thou sufferest us to die for want of bread.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh: for the Egyptians sold every man his field, because the famine prevailed over them: so the land became Pharaohs.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And as for the people, he removed them to tities <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Under the Cities are here comprehended the Villages and Lands belonging to the Territory and Government of each City, for the seed which he gave them was not to be sown in Cities but in the Countrey: but the <ns0:hi>Cities</ns0:hi> onely are here mentioned, because they were sent thither first, either for the conveniency of nourishing them during this Famine out of the publick store<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />houses which were there; or that they might all profess their subjection to the Governments of the several Cities, which was convenient for the management of that numerous and tumultu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous people; or that the Cities might be first and most reple<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nished with inhabitants, as being the principal honour and strength and security of a Kingdom, and that Arts and Trades and Merchandise might flourish, without which the commodi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties of the Country would have been of less price and use. But the Cities being first supplied, the residue, which doubtless was vast, were dispersed in the Countrey.</ns0:note> from one end of the borders of Egypt, even to the <ns0:hi>other</ns0:hi> end thereof <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Far from their na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tive <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>oil and antient Patrimonies, that none of them might plead prescription, but that all might be forced to acknowledge that they owed their estates not to their own wit and industry, nor to their Parents gift, but wholly to the Kings favour, and that the remembrance of their patrimonial Lands might be worn out, and therewith the grief which would arise from their resentment of their loss of them, which probably would be matter of tumults and seditions, to which that people were very prone. And it is probable, that he so disposed of this af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fair, that those who were apt and likely and used to unite to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gether in seditious insurrections, whether kindred or others, should be separated one from another, as far as might be. If any think that <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> dealt hardly with them, and made an ill use of their necessity, he will see how moderately and merci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fully he deals with them, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 24.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 Only the land of the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> Princes.</ns0:note> Priests <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Under this name he understands chiefly those who admini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stred the Worship of the Gods or Idols of <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> and withal those who applied themselves to the study of the arts and vertues, called their <ns0:hi>wisemen</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>magicians.</ns0:hi> Though some understand it of the Princes (as that word sometimes signifies) or Officers of <ns0:hi>Pharaoh,</ns0:hi> who were nourished out of the Kings Treasures. And possibly the same <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> word may here com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prehend both, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the ministers of the King and of their Idols too, for both enjoyed the same priviledges, as <ns0:hi>Diodorus Siculus</ns0:hi> relates. And that the Priests are included, if not mainly in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tended here, will be evident enough to any one that consi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ders the state of <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> how mad that people universally were upon their Idols, how numerous their Priests were and in how great honour and veneration both with Prince and People. Besides, reason of State obliged <ns0:hi>Pharaoh</ns0:hi> to ingage and secure to himself that sort of men which bore so great sway with the old inhabitants of their several places, and were likely to have the same authority with the new inhabitants, to quiet and sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tisfie them at their first change, which must needs be very un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />grateful to them.</ns0:note> bought he not <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Of this immunity of the Priests that an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tient writer, <ns0:hi>Diodorus Siculus,</ns0:hi> makes mention. But this is not to be ascribed to <ns0:hi>Iosephs</ns0:hi> will or choice, for he who abhorred their Idolatry, could not have a kindness for nor would have given encouragement to, the great upholders and promoters of it, but in this he was over-ruled either by <ns0:hi>Pharaohs</ns0:hi> express com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mand, (it being not probable; that so great an interest as that of the Priests should not have friends at Court, or that their friends should not plead for them, or that their pleas and desires should not be granted by an Idolatrous King) or by the Laws of <ns0:hi>E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gypt,</ns0:hi> or by their customs and usages in things of a like nature, which would have the force of a law among them.</ns0:note>: for the Priests had a portion assigned them of Pharaoh. and did eat their portion which Pha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />raoh gave them: wherefore they sold not their lands.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 Then Joseph said unto the people, Behold, I have bought you this day, and your land for Pharaoh: Lo, here is seed for you, and ye shall sow the land <ns0:note n="‖" place="bottom">For this was the last year of the Famine, as was noted before.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 And it shall come to pass in the increase, that you shall give the fifth part unto Pharaoh, and four parts shall be your own <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Whereas he might have reserved four parts to Pharaoh and have allowed them onely the fifth. Herein he shewed both his humanity and kindness in mitigating that hard bar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gain which themselves had made and were necessitated to make, and his prudence, in composing, sweetning, and win<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ning the hearts of the people to the King, and making them pay their tribute for the future with more chearfulness.</ns0:note>, for seed of the field, and for your food, and for them of your housholds, and for food for your little ones.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 And they said, Thou hast saved our lives <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Without thy care and Providence we had all been dead men, and therefore if thou hadst kept us to the first bargain, thou hadst done us more kindness than wrong, much more when thou hast used us with so much equity and clemency.</ns0:note>: let us find grace in the sight of my Lord <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Be thou our friend with <ns0:hi>Pharaoh</ns0:hi> in this and upon all other oc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />casions.</ns0:note>, and we will be Pharaohs servants <ns0:note n="*" place="bottom">To manage his land for him upon the terms which thou hast proposed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And Joseph made it a law over the land of Egypt unto this day, that Pharaoh should have the fifth part <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">That the propriety of the land should be <ns0:hi>Pharaohs,</ns0:hi> and that in token thereof the people should pay the fifth part of the products of it to <ns0:hi>Pharaoh.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>: except the land of the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> Princes.</ns0:note> Priests only, <ns0:hi>which</ns0:hi> became not Pharaohs.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And Israel dwelt in the land of Egypt, in the country of Goshen, and they had possessions <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Lands, not for the dominion or propriety of them, for that rested in <ns0:hi>Pharaoh,</ns0:hi> but for the use and profit of them for their present subsistence.</ns0:note> therein, and grew and multiplyed exceedingly.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt, se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venteen years: so <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the days of the years of his life.</ns0:note> the whole age of Jacob was an hundred fourty and seven years.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 And the time drew <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>igh that Israel must die, and he called his son Joseph, and said unto him, If now I have found grace in thy sight, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 24. 2.</ns0:note> put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Swear to me, as <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 31. that thou wilt do what I am now desiring of thee. See the notes on <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 24. 2. He requires this, not out of any distrust of <ns0:hi>Iosephs</ns0:hi> promise, but partly as a more solemn protestation of his right to, and affection for that promised land: partly as a motive to all his children to have their minds and hearts there even when their bodies were in <ns0:hi>Egypt;</ns0:hi> and partly to give <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> an argument and excuse to <ns0:hi>Pharaoh</ns0:hi> that he might more willingly permit <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> to fulfil his fathers desire because of his own oath.</ns0:note>, and deal <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>that thou wilt deal:</ns0:hi> as the Hebrew <ns0:hi>Vau</ns0:hi> joyned with the future tense is else<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />where used, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 24. 7. and 35. 24. and 51. 15.</ns0:note> kindly and truly <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Kind<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly</ns0:hi> in promising, and <ns0:hi>truly</ns0:hi> in performing thy promise.</ns0:note> with me, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>See</ns0:hi> chap. 50<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 25.</ns0:note> bury me not, I pray thee, in Egypt.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:45" />30 But I will lie with my fathers <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Canaan.</ns0:hi> See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 23. 19. and 25. 9. and 35. 29. Which he desired not so much for himself, as knowing that wherever he was buried, he should rise to Glory; as for his children, to shew his own, and confirm their faith in Gods promise of <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> to discover his high valuation of that land not onely for it self, but as it was a type and pledge of the heavenly inheritance, to keep his childrens minds and hearts loose from <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> a place of so much sin and danger, and fixed upon <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> that they might be more willing to go thither when God called them, by vertue of that inclination which is in most persons to be buried with their Fathers: and in the mean time to declare his detestation of Idolaters, with whom he would have no communion either in life, as far as he could avoid it, or in the place of burial; and on the contrary to profess his communion with his godly Ancestours by his desire to be joyned with them in burial. And for the same reasons <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> desired the translation of his bones thither, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 50. 25.</ns0:note>, and thou shalt carry me out of Egypt, and bury me in their burying-place: and he said, I will do as thou hast said.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 And he said, Swear unto me: and he sware unto him.
